ego.name: Claus Schenk Graf von Stauffenberg
ego.summary: German Wehrmacht officer and a leading figure of the military resistance against National Socialism. He carried out the failed 20 July 1944 bomb attempt on Adolf Hitler and played a central role in the planned coup (Operation Valkyrie).

connections.relationship_description: Father; a senior Württemberg court official who supported and welcomed Claus von Stauffenberg's decision for a military career.
connections.notes: Father served King Wilhelm II of Württemberg as Oberhofmarschall.

connections.relationship_description: Mother; provided a culturally rich, tolerant household and strongly shaped the brothers’ education in literature, music, and theatre.
shared_activities: family life in Stuttgart and summer stays in Lautlingen
connections.notes: She was Protestant while the children were raised Catholic.

connections.person_name: Konrad Maria Schenk Graf von Stauffenberg
connections.relationship_description: Twin brother who died one day after birth, shaping the immediate family context at Claus's birth.
connections.notes: Relationship is biographical rather than interactive due to Konrad's immediate death.

connections.relationship_description: Older brother; together they entered the Stefan George circle and shared parts of the intellectual milieu that influenced Claus's worldview.
shared_activities: participation in the Stefan George circle and the 'Secret Germany' idea
connections.notes: Berthold later referenced Claus's views during Gestapo interrogation (as noted in the article).

connections.relationship_description: Older brother; shared youth and early intellectual formation including contact with Stefan George and related cultural ideals.
shared_activities: association with the Stefan George circle
connections.notes: The brothers are described as entering George's close circle together.

connections.relationship_description: Poet and guiding influence; introduced in 1923, and the George Circle’s “Secret Germany” ideal shaped Stauffenberg’s cultural-ethical outlook.
shared_activities: correspondence (including a 1933 letter mentioned in the article)
connections.notes: The article describes Stauffenberg's lifelong devotion to George's legacy.

connections.relationship_description: Fellow officer in the 17th Bavarian Cavalry Regiment in Bamberg; Stauffenberg befriended him during early service as a young officer.
shared_activities: service in the 17th Bavarian Cavalry Regiment (Bamberg)
connections.notes: Identified as the son of a famous surgeon in the article.

connections.relationship_description: Reich President during the last Weimar years; a key political backdrop to Hitler’s rise that framed debates within the officer corps.
shared_activities: Hindenburg’s office as a framework for the transition to Hitler’s rule
connections.notes: No direct personal interaction is evidenced in the provided extracts; relationship is political/structural.

connections.relationship_description: Wife (married 1933); mother of his five children and the closest personal anchor in his adult life.
shared_activities: correspondence during wartime (letters referenced in secondary discussion on his views)
connections.notes: The article lists her later civic engagement in/around Bamberg and her death in 2006.

connections.relationship_description: Head of state and commander-in-chief against whom Stauffenberg’s resistance turned; Stauffenberg placed the bomb at the Wolf’s Lair on 20 July 1944 to kill Hitler and trigger a coup.
shared_activities: Stauffenberg’s evolving stance toward the regime (initial approval in 1933, later resistance)
connections.notes: Interaction is institutional and adversarial rather than personal; Stauffenberg had access to Hitler’s briefings as staff officer in 1944.

connections.person_name: Berthold Maria Schenk Graf von Stauffenberg
connections.relationship_description: Son; one of five children from the marriage to Nina von Lerchenfeld.
connections.notes: The article notes he later became a Bundeswehr generalmajor.

connections.relationship_description: Close collaborator from General Staff training onward; one of Stauffenberg’s most trusted associates and executed with him after the failed coup.
shared_activities: General Staff training contacts (War Academy, Berlin)
drafting/issuing Valkyrie-related orders from the Bendlerblock
connections.notes: The Stauffenberg article highlights his early professional ties to Mertz during War Academy training.

connections.relationship_description: Met during General Staff training in Berlin; later part of the wider military resistance network and involved in Paris actions connected to Valkyrie plans.
shared_activities: General Staff training at the War Academy (Berlin)
resistance-related coordination (Paris network referenced in 20 July account)
connections.notes: The Stauffenberg article explicitly names Finckh as an early Berlin professional contact.

connections.relationship_description: Divisional superior when Stauffenberg served as a general staff officer (1b) in the 1st Light Division in 1938; Hoepner was his immediate commanding general.
shared_activities: staff work in the 1st Light Division
connections.notes: Hoepner later became associated with anti-Hitler resistance circles (contextual in related article on 20 July plot).

connections.relationship_description: Co-leading figure of the military resistance; Stauffenberg became central alongside Tresckow from 1942 onward, and they jointly advanced assassination/coup planning.
shared_activities: adaptation and planning around Operation Valkyrie (as part of the resistance network)
connections.notes: Related article describes Tresckow as central until Stauffenberg took a leading operational role in 1943/44.

connections.relationship_description: Key co-conspirator; worked with Stauffenberg in the Bendlerblock to trigger Operation Valkyrie and was executed alongside him after the coup failed.
shared_activities: planning and implementing coup preparations within the Ersatzheer
attempted activation of Operation Valkyrie on 20 July 1944
connections.notes: Olbricht’s biography notes he brought Stauffenberg in as a key staff member for the coup plan.

connections.relationship_description: Stauffenberg’s adjutant and confidant during the 20 July attempt; accompanied him to the Wolf's Lair and returned to Berlin for Valkyrie implementation; executed with him.
connections.notes: The 20 July article describes Haeften assisting Stauffenberg while arming the bomb due to Stauffenberg’s injuries.

connections.relationship_description: Senior figure of the anti-Hitler opposition; designated as head of state in coup plans, present in the Bendlerblock during the coup attempt, and died after its failure.
connections.notes: Beck was intended as 'Staatsoberhaupt' in planning described in the 20 July article.

connections.relationship_description: Cousin; involved in coordinating resistance and liaison between Berlin and the Paris network connected to 20 July plans.
shared_activities: coordination between Berlin resistance circle and Paris actions related to Valkyrie
connections.notes: The Stauffenberg article identifies Hofacker as a cousin; the 20 July article describes his Paris coordinating role.

connections.relationship_description: Commander of the Replacement Army and Stauffenberg’s superior in 1944; refused the coup once Hitler’s survival was clear and ordered the executions.
shared_activities: Ersatzheer staff work (Bendlerblock chain of command)
connections.notes: Fromm’s biography notes he had tolerated conspiratorial planning but chose self-protection once the plot appeared to fail.

category_summaries.summary: Stauffenberg’s network includes a strongly documented core family: both parents, siblings (notably Berthold and Alexander), his wife Nina, and children. Family background and aristocratic-Catholic upbringing shaped his early career choices and cultural formation.

Professional ties cluster around Wehrmacht staff work and, in 1944, the Replacement Army and Bendlerblock. The network’s key line runs through co-conspirators (Olbricht, Quirnheim, Haeften), senior opposition figures (Beck), and decisive superiors (Fromm).
A small set of peer friendships (e.g., within the Bamberg cavalry milieu) hints at the officer-corps social fabric behind later trust networks.

An important non-military strand is his long-lasting intellectual and aesthetic affiliation with the Stefan George circle. George’s mentorship and the 'Secret Germany' ideal provided a cultural-ethical framework that Stauffenberg and his brothers carried into adulthood.
